utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. I repeat my previous objection about asking the witness about what other people have said. The witness's opinion about what other persons may have said or may not have said or may say in future is not a proper question. It is improper asking the witness about what other people said, his opinion on what other people said, his knowledge on other people having said whatever. If the defence wants to introduce a statement of somebody else, it cannot do that through a witness who is not the person who made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are asking if Mirko Babic was the person who cooperated with distributing the arms in his village as alleged by somebody else. I will introduce both these statements into evidence for the defence as we speak, if the court would like. I have one question from this statement and two questions from this statement. They are both very relevant. Mr Babic has stated that he is not politically active, that he has no involvement whatsoever with the political environment in his community, and everybody -- all the other statements indicate that yes, he was very active in organising a resistance. I will introduce these for the court's review immediately after I question him from them. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Kindly repeat your question and let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will try. So if Risto Vukalo says that you, Mirko Babic, and Miro Duricic were responsible for cooperating with Strahinja Zivak in distributing the arms from the shipments, he would be lying; is that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Please allow me. Risto Vukalo is cousin through my wife's sister. So he is a kin. I did not cooperate with Strahinja. Let them gossip if they come here. You will see. They'll tell you what they were saying, but I doubt very much. It was not true, but where does this come from? I don't know. Not from Risto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is that he would be lying if he made that statement? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would like to introduce this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You cannot produce it in court in order to have a statement before us. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You cannot introduce somebody's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I have one more question also. So if Dusko Bendjo said he gave you an M48 rifle, he would be lying, would he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object calling a liar anybody who might or might not be a witness in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I apologise. He would be saying an untruth, would he not; yes?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Yes if he also said that the contacts for arming the residents of Bijelovcina were Slobo Babic and Mirko Babic -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is rejected all times. You do not go about repeating what a witness has rejected differently. He has rejected that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. So he is saying that all of these statements are incorrect. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One more question. Mr Babic, in your statement of February 20th 1996 you stated that you were a permanent invalid, did you not?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I pass the witness, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The witness is ready for re-examination, if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Babic, did Slobodan Babic receive any medical care during the days he was in number 22?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: I didn't see that anybody came to help him. I did not see and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So you did not have any occasion to observe anything concerning Mr Slobodan Babic during those days?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean you did not see anything particular?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Another question, Mr Babic: about Mr Branko Gotovac, when he was brought to the infirmary, was he ever brought back to hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Yes, he was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: And do you remember how did he return to hangar 6 after the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: He was returned. He complained about some pain in the stomach and shoulders, as far as I can recall. He complained.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: All right. My last question now: did you yourself, with your own eyes, have you ever yourself seen Ivan Azinovic taken out from the hangar by Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: That I did not see. I only know that he disappeared some time in the evening and in the morning he was not there but who took him I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: I have finished, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I promise I have three questions on re-cross, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is re-cross? He is not your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, but -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He is not your witness. You say you are familiar with the Common Law cross-examination and Common Law trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. May I respond? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You cannot, please. You can only re-examine your own witness, not another witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, that is not the way it is in our country. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I know your country a little bit. It is that way. You do not go around re-examining other people's witnesses. I think that is all for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can I make it clear for my clarification so I understand: he does direct; we do cross; he does re-direct, so he gets the last word even though he has the burden of proof? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: When it comes to your own witness, you have to re-examine. He does not re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then we would like to ask that this witness be available to recall him in the defence case, because we have certainly not completed our questioning of him. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If we continue this, there will be no end to this trial if everyone who comes is kept aside to enable you, I suppose, after your style of cross-examination, who is kept aside for you. Then there will be no end for it. You have had enough time and I kept on at every one of you. You have had enough time to cross-examine. I think that is a normal situation. The witness can stand down.

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Shall we continue? Ladies and gentlemen, shall we continue? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You mean with the witness? We have nothing for him.

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Am I going to come back here? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, it depends on the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Am I going to come back here? Can I say thank you. I would like to say thank you, if it is over. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is not completely, because there is still the medical examination of your leg. The doctor still has to verify your injury. The doctor still has to verify your injury, whether there was an actual injury at the time you complained you were burned or something else. So you have to wait a little bit. (Pause). You can now stand down.

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr Ostberg, what is your next ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I now ask leave from the Trial Chamber to bring a witness who is not on the witness list. utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please, the court, before this witness may I present an argument to the court regarding presentation of evidence? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not know. Perhaps I might clarify a few things. I do not know what you want to say, but I think if you all remember, and I am sure you do, Article 15 of the Statute establishes in the tribunal first, the judges of the tribunal, the power to make rules. It is on the rules made by the judges of the tribunal that we are operating. In making the rules, the judges took active consideration of all the systems of the continents, each of the continents, and there are several, and the Common Law systems, and not to waste your time, let me go straight to the issue about presentation of evidence at Rule 85. It is very clear. I was surprised when Ms McMurrey thought otherwise. Now apart from presenting -- showing of evidence, it even goes on, which is (a) -- if you read it, it is very clear. It says: "Each party is entitled to call witnesses and present evidence unless otherwise directed by the Trial Chamber in the interests of justice. Evidence at the trial shall be presented in the following sequence: evidence for the prosecution; evidence for the defence; prosecution evidence in rebuttal; defence evidence in rejoinder; evidence by the Trial Chamber pursuant to rule 98." Then it goes forward in (b) to tell you what should be done in case of leading witnesses. It says: "Examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination shall be allowed in each case. It shall be for the party calling a witness to examine him in chief, but a judge must not at any stage put any question to the witness." Now even in respect of re-examination the tradition of the Common Law which we all know is that you can only re-examine on matters arising from cross-examination. It is not at large. Nobody just goes about asking whatever questions they like. Now cross-examination may be at large, but it should be relevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber. So I do not know what other systems -- obviously when it becomes necessary, if there are any gaps in our own procedure and we find that in the interests of justice it is necessary to resort to other systems, we will do that. We would not allow any gaps in our rules to stop us doing justice in any case before us, but for the time being I have not discovered, and the Trial Chamber itself has not discovered, any gap in the question of examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination. So that is what we are obliged to follow: Mr O'Sullivan. Let us hear what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, it is precisely on (b) of Rule 85, the first sentence ending: "Re-examination shall be allowed in each case." In other words re-examination in re-direct and re-cross, scope being limited in each case, the scope of re-examination in this case limited for clarification on the in-chief. I submit that re-cross is limited to the re-examination and that is consistent, I would submit, with the way (a) is framed, beginning with prosecution, defence, rebuttal and rejoinder. The defence has the last word. That is tied in as well with final arguments. The last word is given to the defence, all of which flows from the burden of proof, which is clearly on the prosecutor. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is your interpretation of it. My interpretation of it, which we are familiar with, is that the prosecution or the person leading evidence is entitled to re-examine his witness, not the person cross-examining. That is the principle involved in re-examination. He will examine in areas which arose out of cross-examination. Now let us have the witness: please let him swear the witness. utterances.speaker: MR TURONE

utterances.speaker: how many persons from his village were taken to
utterances.text: I reached my mother-in-law's and my brother-in-law, Trile, and another one, Milorad, was there. Our family was there. Then I heard someone calling on the loudspeaker my husband Lazar to surrender, but he could not hear because he had already fled. He was not with me and my mother-in-law at that moment, and when night fell they kept shooting until night. Then my mother-in-law suggested that we go hide in the caves. There were a number of caves there between her house and my brother-in-law, Miso's, but I headed for the village because my husband and son were not there. With Jagoda Manigoda, called 'Zaga', I headed for my uncle's house, my Uncle Lazar, and I saw Ranko Kuljanin, called 'Majstor'. I asked him about my husband and son and he said they were there. My house was already on fire. My son hugged me and said: "Do not worry, mother. We'll make a new and better one if we survive". I said: "Never mind, so long as you are alive. Where is Lazar?" Then I saw him, my husband. That night we went towards Cerici. We were fleeing in the woods but many houses were on fire. Eight or nine Serb houses were burning -- Vojo Dekic's house on the right side of the Neretva. Then Jovo -- I can't remember his surname; he is from Montenegro. Then Jovo Arnautovic's house; my house; of late Mico Cecez's house -- he was a chimney sweep; Milijan Cecez's; Dusan Cecez's house, an old one in the village; some other houses I can't remember just at this moment. Bijelovcina had already been attacked too. At that moment two people from Bijelovcina got killed, and the night when our village was attacked Rajko Ninkovic got killed first. Then somebody told me about these two people from Bijelovcina who got killed. I didn't know them. We kept retreating in the direction of Cerici. Sefko Niksic called out "Lazar" on the loudspeaker: "Lazar, surrender. We won't do anything", but Lazar had gone. I don't know where. We stayed on. Then very heavy shooting started. We kept quiet. They hurled something very powerful very close to our cave. The whole cave shook. Rocks were falling on us. There were two small children, the children of Ferid Asanovic and his wife -- his wife was Serbian -- and we were afraid what would happen to those children. So we didn't dare stay on, and these bullets were falling on us all day until 3.30. Then it quietened down a bit. Then we went to my brother-in-law Trile's house. His house was still standing. We went into his cellar and I waited there. Two or three nights we spent there. On 25th they attacked Bradina and they took all the population, mostly men, probably women too. On 27th there was another attack on Donje Selo. They again reached my house. What was left of it they set fire to. Jelka Savic, she's a relative of mine, and she said: "Sefko Niksic is calling you and Trile", my brother-in-law, "to come", and we set out towards Aunt Milka's house. She had a house on the hill. They intercepted us, and she said that Niksic had said if we didn't come, we would get a bullet. They started beating Trile. I couldn't watch it and Ibrahim Duro -- and he is also some kind of a godson -- he said: "Do not fear. Dusko is with us." Dusko is my son. "We won't hurt him." So I headed with him to the cooperative centre. We crossed the railway line. They put us under the window of Maxim Igoda's house and I saw Trile all bloody. He had a cut on his forehead.
